posts.headline: Flock just changed its surveillance rules
posts.subhead: The license plate camera network cut how long it stores your movements — with a catch.
changes: Default data retention drops from 30 days to 7 days.
But existing agencies keep their current period unless they opt in.
Cities can now block outside agencies from searching their cameras for immigration enforcement.
Misuse detection becomes mandatory for all police customers by the end of 2026.
Abnormal search patterns will trigger an automatic lockout pending administrator review.
Every search will require a case number, and multi-factor login is now mandatory.
posts.verdict_text: The audit requirements are real. But the 7-day retention is a recommendation, not a switch. How long your movements are stored still depends on your city council, not on Flock.
actions: Look up your police department's Flock Transparency Portal.
Ask your city council: 7-day retention, or still 30?
Check deflock.org for cameras mapped near you.
posts.caption:
Flock Safety runs one of the largest license plate camera networks in the country — tens of thousands of readers logging where cars go. After a year of reporting on officers misusing the system, the company just announced a package of changes.

What's new: default data retention drops from 30 days to 7. Misuse detection becomes mandatory for every law enforcement customer by the end of 2026, with automatic lockouts for abnormal search patterns. Case codes become required on every search. Multi-factor authentication is now mandatory. An outside firm, Bishop Fox, is auditing the products with findings promised in September.

The catch: the 7-day retention is a recommendation, not a default that flips for everyone. Existing agencies keep their current period unless they opt in. Civil liberties groups have called the package an improvement wrapped around the same underlying "trust us" model.

So the useful move isn't watching Flock — it's checking your own city. Most agencies publish a Flock Transparency Portal showing retention, sharing partners, and search volume. Worth asking whether yours has turned on offense filtering, too — that's the setting that limits what outside departments can search your cameras for.

posts.caption: Amazon updated its Conditions of Use on August 14, 2026, replacing a straightforward court-dispute clause with a detailed mandatory arbitration system. Under the new terms, if you have a complaint about Amazon — a bad charge, a faulty product, a policy dispute — you can no longer take it to a regular court with a judge or jury. Instead, you must first contact customer service and negotiate for up to 60 days, then go through a JAMS arbitration process. A new class-action waiver means you cannot join other customers in a lawsuit against Amazon; each person must fight their case alone. The only notable carve-out is for personal injury or property damage from a product, which will now be governed by the law of the state where the harm occurred. If you ever need to dispute something with Amazon, know that your legal options have narrowed considerably.

🚨 AMAZON POLICY UPDATE

Amazon now uses your data to train AI

WHAT CHANGED:
• Amazon now explicitly uses your data to develop and deploy generative AI models.
• Linking your Amazon account to a third-party via Login with Amazon is now listed as a data source.
• Amazon replaced 'search results and Sponsored Links' with broader ad-interaction tracking on third-party sites and apps.
• Amazon now collects advertising identifiers and data from third parties to improve its services.

OUR VERDICT: IMPORTANT
The new AI training clause and expanded ad-tracking language meaningfully broaden how Amazon can use your personal data.

WHAT YOU CAN DO:
→ Review Amazon's Generative AI Development Disclosure linked in the policy.
→ Check your ad preferences and opt out of interest-based ads at amazon.com/ibanotice.
→ Avoid linking your Amazon account to third-party apps unless necessary.
